instrument.title: Expert study on generated programming exercises
instrument.materiality_rule: Answer **No** if the problem would plausibly cost an introductory programming student noticeable time, lead to a wrong submission, or send them to a tutor. If the issue is cosmetic and does none of these, answer **Yes**.

How much do you agree with this statement? “AI-generated exercises can, in principle, be suitable for teaching.”

pages.title: Purpose of the study
pages.body:
Thank you for taking part. We study how well an AI pipeline generates programming exercises
for introductory programming courses.

Each exercise starts from a **brief** that an instructor wrote: the learning objective, what
the students already know and what they have not learned yet, and the expected effort. From
the brief, the pipeline generated a complete exercise: a problem statement, a template that
students start from, a sample solution, and tests. The tests automatically assess students’ submissions (autograding). Every exercise you see has been checked
automatically: it compiles, its sample solution passes all its tests, and its template passes
none of them. We ask you to judge whether the exercise is suitable for teaching.

Neither you nor the other raters know which model the AI pipeline used for an exercise. Please do not
discuss the exercises with anyone until we tell you that the study has closed.

pages.title: How a rating works
pages.body:
You rate each exercise in four parts, about 18 minutes per exercise. Each part
adds material, and earlier material stays open:

| Part | You see | You rate |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | The problem statement and the brief it was generated from | Clarity |
| B | + the template and the solution changes | Solvability, fit with the brief, scope, scaffolding |
| C | + the tests and their failure messages | Feedback, readiness |
| D | + the automatic findings | Automatic findings, readiness again |

You cannot go back to an earlier part. If later material changes your view, note it under
*Remarks on earlier answers* in Part D. On your first exercise, a short tour shows you where
everything is.

pages.title: Answering the questions
pages.body:
You answer most questions with Yes or No; a few also offer N/A. When your answer points to a
problem, a short field asks where it is or why. For borderline cases, the materiality rule
applies:

> Answer **No** if the problem would plausibly cost an introductory programming student noticeable time, lead to a wrong submission, or send them to a tutor. If the issue is cosmetic and does none of these, answer **Yes**.

| Situation | Question | Answer | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| "recieve" is misspelled in the problem statement | CL2 | Yes | A cosmetic issue |
| The problem statement and the template ask for the average but do not say how to round it, and the sample solution rounds it to two decimal places | SO1 | No | Leads to a wrong submission |
| The problem statement says "ignore invalid entries" without saying whether an empty name is invalid | CL1 | No | Two reasonable readings |
| The test `countsOnlyActiveMembers` fails with "expected: <3> but was: <0>" | FB1 | Yes | The test name explains the problem |
| Several tests are named `test1` to `test5` and have no messages | FB1 | No | The student cannot tell what is wrong |

pages.title: Meaning of the readiness levels
pages.body:
Twice per exercise, you rate how much work you would need before you could use it in an
introductory programming course. These examples serve as anchors:

| Level | Meaning | Typical example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 5 · Use as is | No change needed | You would give the exercise to your students today. |
| 4 · Minor edits | Wording or formatting only | You clarify a sentence or add the expected output format to the problem statement. |
| 3 · Moderate edits | Local changes; the design stays | You add failure messages to a few tests, rename a misleading stub, or fix one rule and its test. |
| 2 · Major revision | Parts must be redesigned | The template already solves the core concept, or half of the tasks have no tests. |
| 1 · Discard | Writing it from scratch is faster | The exercise targets a different topic or level. |

Rate your own effort as an instructor; the other questions cover the effort of students.

questionnaire.title: Rating
questionnaire.perspective: Answer as an instructor who decides whether to give this exercise to the students of an introductory programming course.

parts.title: Problem statement
parts.opens: Read the problem statement and the brief it was generated from.

items.prompt: Is every required behaviour stated so that only one reasonable reading exists?
items.look_for: a rule two competent students would implement differently ("sort the items" without key or direction, an inclusive or exclusive bound); an example whose result does not follow from the stated rule.

detail.label: Where
detail.hint: A task or a sentence is enough.

items.prompt: Is the problem statement easy to understand for an introductory programming student?
items.look_for: undefined jargon; requirements buried in the narrative; a problem statement much longer or denser than the exercise warrants.

detail.label: Where
detail.hint: A task or a sentence is enough.

parts.title: Template and solution changes
parts.opens: Skim the template students start from: which files they get, which stubs they complete, and what the comments say. The solution changes show what students add or change; you do not need to check them line by line.

items.prompt: Do the problem statement and the template tell students everything they need to produce the expected results, without seeing the tests?
items.look_for: an edge case mentioned without its expected result; an output that must match exactly (message text, number format, ordering) but is not given verbatim.

detail.label: Where
detail.hint: A task, a sentence, or a file is enough.

items.prompt: Does the exercise practise the concept or learning objective named in the brief?

detail.label: Where
detail.hint: A task, a sentence, or a file is enough.

items.prompt: Must students actually apply the target concept to solve the exercise?
items.look_for: the concept is already implemented in the template; a plain approach solves the exercise equally well and the problem statement does not rule it out (a recursion exercise solvable with a simple loop).

detail.label: Where
detail.hint: A task, a sentence, or a file is enough.

options.label: N/A, the brief names no specific concept

items.prompt: Does the exercise honour the explicit requirements of the brief?
items.look_for: a requested diagram, edge case, determinism constraint, given type, or prerequisite that the exercise ignores or exceeds.

items.prompt: Is the scenario sensible and motivating for the exercise?
items.look_for: a context bolted onto an unrelated computation; contrived rules presented as realistic; wrong domain facts; a scenario that excludes or stereotypes groups of students.

detail.label: Where
detail.hint: A task, a sentence, or a file is enough.

items.prompt: Is the scope right: enough work to practise the concept, and at most 60 minutes for a student at this point in the course?
items.note: Judge from the brief and the solution changes.

choices.label: Too little to practise the concept

items.prompt: Does the template give the right amount of support, so that the students' effort goes to the target concept?
items.look_for: students must write boilerplate the exercise does not aim to teach (visible in the solution changes); so much is given that little remains; stubs whose purpose is unclear.

detail.label: Where
detail.hint: A task, a sentence, or a file is enough.

items.prompt: Do the tasks of the problem statement form useful steps, so that students see their partial progress?
items.look_for: one task for a multi-part exercise; a task that cannot be attempted before a later one; task titles that do not say what to do.

detail.label: Where
detail.hint: A task, a sentence, or a file is enough.

items.prompt: Other pedagogical issues in Parts A and B

parts.title: Tests
parts.opens: Read each task's tests and the message a student sees when one fails. Where possible, the message comes from a wrong variant of the sample solution, as a student's mistake would produce it; otherwise it is the message on the template. Test code is not shown.

items.prompt: Would a student who fails a test learn from its name and message what is wrong, without being handed the solution?
items.look_for: a test whose name and message together do not say what is wrong (`test1` failing with only "expected: <3> but was: <0>"); messages that spell out the code to write.
